newsitem.title: BELGIUM: German gold move highlights EU dilemma.
newsitem.headline: German gold move highlights EU dilemma.

text.p: German Finance Minister Theo Waigel's controversial plan to revalue gold as a way of qualifying for the single currency goes to the heart of the dilemma facing the European Union as monetary union approaches.
But it is Italy, not Germany, that is the key.

In short, Bonn has to qualify for economic and monetary union (EMU) on January 1, 1999, without any question of doubt if it is to keep lesser economies -- notably Rome's -- from entering and watering down the new currency's credibility.

Germany said on Thursday it expected an 18 billion mark ($10.6 billion) tax revenue shortfall this year, throwing into question its ability to meet the EMU goal of a 1997 deficit of no more than three percent of Gross Domestic Product.
EU officials and market analysts said Waigel's proposals for meeting the crisis -- including revaluing the Bundesbank's gold -- were proof positive that Germany was desperate to meet the criteria.
"Everyone expects that by hook or by crook Germany will make it," said one London-based economist.
Delay of EMU, an issue much debated a few months ago, was not in the cards, they said.
The snag for Germany, however, is that it has to meet the criteria without opening the door to countries considered less worthy. Without Germany, the whole EMU project would founder.

The European Union has been telling Italy indirectly that it is not going to make it. On Monday, for example, EU finance ministers sent Rome a stinging review of the state of Italian government finances.
German moneymen, in particular, are adamant that Italy is not ready.

But Rome has got closer than many expected. The European Commission sees it only 0.2 percent above the key three percent deficit/GDP criterion this year, but its outlook for 1998 is less optimistic, putting Italy's deficit at 3.9 percent of GDP.
Any fudge by Germany -- by employing "creative accounting", for example -- would mean Italy could also claim dispensation from the Maastricht Treaty's tough rules.
"You've seen headlines with (Italy) highlighting the dilemma," the economist said.
Possibly with a degree Schadenfreude, Italy has been reminding Germany of its commitments. Foreign Minister Lamberto Dini referred to accounting gimmicks on Thursday.
Analysts in Italy see the Waigel move as a help to Italy's chances -- just what the German moneymen feared.
